clue.text: The Northern cream's gathered – its inhabitants would say!

definitions.text: The Northern cream's gathered – its inhabitants would say!

indicators.note: things gathered are collected up and bunched together any old way, so these letters come out in a new arrangement

blocks.note: taken as written
N is the abbreviation for northern
taken as written, with the S of the apostrophe

explanation.surface: Proud locals boast that the best of the North has collected in their city.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cream' sounds like dairy, but it means the elite; the whole clue is also the definition, the Mancunians' own claim that the North's best people gather there.
explanation.definitionFit: A big northern English city whose residents are famously proud, so they would claim the finest northerners have collected there.

indicators.note: to introduce something is to put it in front, so the second item named here comes first in the answer

blocks.note: short for magazine
the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A single publication presents a feature on some wise men.
explanation.walkthrough: The order is flipped: the publication introduces the one, so the magazine part leads.
explanation.definitionFit: The Magi are the three wise men of the Nativity story who brought gifts to the infant Jesus.

blocks.note: first meaning: mad, out of one's mind
second meaning: an exclamation of annoyance or dismay

explanation.walkthrough: It reads like someone reacting in horror to being called mad; really it is two separate meanings of one short word.
explanation.definitionFit: The word serves as slang for being insane and also as an exasperated interjection when something goes wrong.

indicators.note: a drunk person stumbles about unsteadily, so these letters lurch out of their order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A cheerful Ray strums a harp after a few drinks.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Merry' doubles as a word for tipsy, which suits the drunken harpist, but here it means simply very cheerful.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom describes someone extremely contented and cheerful, a colourful equivalent of the single adjective.

clue.text: Mouldy buns leading to runs in a French holiday's discomfort?

indicators.note: mouldy food has gone off and lost its shape, so these letters decay into a new order
one thing placed within another, so these letters sit inside the next piece

blocks.note: taken as written
un is the French for 'a'
R is the cricket scoring abbreviation for runs

explanation.surface: Stale bread and a bout of diarrhoea spoil someone's holiday in France.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Runs' looks like a stomach upset, but it is just the cricket letter; the shuffled bread comes first, then the French article wrapped round that letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Reddened, painful skin from too much exposure to strong sunshine is a classic complaint on a beach trip.

indicators.note: something beaten is knocked about and battered out of shape, so these letters are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: The most aggressive, goading team ends up losing the match.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Side' looks like it could give EDGE by synonym, but it is only raw letters for the shuffle.
explanation.definitionFit: Edgy art or comedy is daring and challenging, so the superlative describes whatever is most daring or likely to offend.

clue.text: Incredulous utterance, Anglo-Saxon, loud: Everyman's entertained

indicators.note: a guest who is entertained is taken into someone's home, so this letter is held between the others

blocks.note: the standard abbreviation for Anglo-Saxon
the setter, Everyman, refers to themself as I
f, forte, is the musical direction for loud

explanation.surface: A loud, disbelieving remark is made by an Anglo-Saxon who has the setter round as a guest.
explanation.walkthrough: The setter's name stands for the first person; that letter sits between the two abbreviations, hosted by them.
explanation.definitionFit: Said sarcastically, the phrase is a scornful exclamation meaning that something is highly unlikely or unbelievable.

clue.text: What's spoken extensively: Romania, Bosnia (obviously), Czech Republic (officially accepted) – that's just for starters!

definitions.text: What's spoken extensively: Romania, Bosnia (obviously), Czech Republic (officially accepted) – that's just for starters!

indicators.note: starters are the opening course, so only the opening letter of each word is wanted

blocks.clueFragment: spoken extensively: Romania, Bosnia (obviously), Czech Republic (officially accepted) – that's
blocks.note: the initial letters of these ten words

explanation.surface: A tongue widely spoken in Bosnia and nearby, listed with some dubious geography.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue defines a Balkan language while its words' initials spell it out; the parenthetical asides are there only to supply letters, and Romania and the Czech Republic are a joke.
explanation.definitionFit: The South Slavic language of the former Yugoslavia, widely used in Bosnia, Serbia, Croatia and Montenegro.

clue.text: Prepared fresh fig in child's fare

indicators.note: food that is prepared is chopped and arranged, so these letters are reworked into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A fresh fig is cut up and served as part of a kid's meal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In' is part of the letters to be shuffled, not a container signal. A fish finger is the British name for a fish stick.
explanation.definitionFit: Breaded strips of fish are a staple of children's teatime menus in Britain, so they are typical kids' food.

clue.text: Fire outfit with old German first

indicators.note: this word says which of the last two pieces goes in front of the other

blocks.note: a getup is a set of clothes
and means 'with', in addition
G is the abbreviation for German
O is the abbreviation for old

explanation.surface: A firing order for a uniform with an elderly German in front.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fire' looks like a verb or a blaze, but it is the noun for zeal; the German letter is placed ahead of the old one.
explanation.definitionFit: Fire can mean passion or vigour, and the phrase is an informal noun for energy and drive.

indicators.note: at regular intervals, so every other letter is taken and the rest skipped

blocks.note: the second, fourth, sixth and eighth letters

explanation.surface: Someone habitually describes a series of conjuring tricks.
explanation.walkthrough: Take the even-numbered letters of the single word.
explanation.definitionFit: Arts in the plural can mean cunning wiles or crafty devices, as in a seducer's arts.

clue.text: Wholesaler's current account with booze comedian's drunk

indicators.note: what is drunk is swallowed down, so one piece ends up inside the other

blocks.note: C/A is the banking abbreviation for a current account
a shandy is beer mixed with lemonade
Jimmy Carr is a British comedian

explanation.surface: A trader's bank account shows spending on drink, and a comedian has got drunk.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Comedian's drunk' reads as a tipsy comic, but it means the comedian has been drunk by the booze, i.e. swallowed into it. Jimmy Carr is a well-known British stand-up.
explanation.definitionFit: A cash-and-carry is a wholesale warehouse where trade buyers pay on the spot and take goods away themselves.

clue.text: Solver, doubtful: 'Weary of France? That's not right'

indicators.note: something doubtful is unsettled and uncertain, so these letters are not fixed in their order

blocks.note: the setter addresses the solver as you
taken as written
F is the international vehicle code for France

explanation.surface: A sceptical solver asks whether being tired of France is really wrong.
explanation.walkthrough: The solver is 'you', followed by a jumble of the quoted words plus France's letter.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is a colloquial way of telling someone their guess is badly mistaken, the same as saying they are wrong.

indicators.note: something struck is hit and knocked about, so these letters are jolted into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A local strikes oil and gets a great deal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Struck oil' is a ready-made phrase about finding wealth, which hides that 'struck' is the shuffle signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words describe people or things that have been in a place from the earliest times, indigenous inhabitants.

clue.text: Hearing positive little thing being discussed

blocks.note: an inquest is a judicial hearing into a death
an ion is a tiny charged particle, which may be positive

explanation.surface: Something small and encouraging is the topic of a hearing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hearing' tempts toward a sound-alike, but it is the legal sense, an official inquiry.
explanation.definitionFit: The matter in question is the one currently under consideration, the topic of the debate.

indicators.note: something trapped is caught and held inside, so this letter goes within the other piece

blocks.note: British slang for precisely right, spot on
S is the abbreviation for son

explanation.surface: A boy has caught some rabbits, exactly as planned.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rabbits' looks like the animals the son caught, but it is the verb. To rabbit and to bang on are British slang for talking at tedious length.
explanation.definitionFit: To rabbit is to chatter on interminably, and bangs on is the same idiom for droning about something.

indicators.note: to cover something is to lie over and conceal it, so the letters are concealed within these words

blocks.note: the letters run across the three words

explanation.surface: A woman's analysis covers the topic of city-states.
explanation.walkthrough: 'City state' looks like one political term; split it, and the second word starts the run of letters.
explanation.definitionFit: This is an older spelling of Tehran, the capital city of Iran.

indicators.note: something spoken is said out loud, so we want a word by its sound not its spelling

blocks.note: to rue is to regret
a barb is a cutting remark

explanation.surface: Someone wishes they had not said a hurtful remark, now dismissed as rubbish.
explanation.walkthrough: The regret word is said, then spelt as the start of the vegetable's name.
explanation.definitionFit: In British slang the word means drivel, from actors murmuring it to fake background chatter on stage.

indicators.note: without a heart means the middle letter is cut out

blocks.note: the word with its central letter removed
Muhammad Ali, the boxer

explanation.surface: A cruel boxer is described as South Asian.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Being heartless' looks like a description of the fighter, but 'Being' is the word that loses its heart.
explanation.definitionFit: A Bengali is a person from Bengal, a region split between Bangladesh and India in South Asia.

clue.text: Troglodyte's back to front in dad's happy place?

indicators.note: the rear part of the word is moved round to the front

blocks.note: a troglodyte is a cave dweller

explanation.surface: A cave-dweller is turned around inside the place where dad feels happiest.
explanation.walkthrough: Swap the two halves of the cave dweller: the back part becomes the front.
explanation.definitionFit: A man cave is a room such as a shed or den kept as a personal retreat for a man, so father's refuge.

blocks.note: mam is a dialect word for mother
a moth is an insect

explanation.surface: A mother remarks that some bug is huge.
explanation.walkthrough: Mam is the northern English and Welsh word for mum.
explanation.definitionFit: Named after the huge extinct elephant, the adjective means gigantic or vast.

blocks.note: G is the abbreviation for good
astronomic means enormously great

explanation.surface: A food lover gives a short verdict on a meal: good, great.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gourmet' looks like a noun, a person, but it is used as an adjective here, as in gourmet cooking.
explanation.definitionFit: Both adjectives relate to fine food and the art of eating well.

clue.text: Stakes raised: it's hot in Sicily

indicators.note: in a down clue, lifting something up turns it so it reads from bottom to top

blocks.note: an ante is a stake put up before a poker hand

explanation.surface: A poker player raising the bets notes the Sicilian heat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Raised' looks like a poker term going with stakes, but it turns the word upwards.
explanation.definitionFit: Etna is the active volcano on Sicily, so a place that is literally hot with molten rock.

indicators.note: something that happens now and then is intermittent, so only every other letter is taken

blocks.note: the even-placed letters of the word

explanation.surface: A firm occasionally hires people who make wordplay jokes.
explanation.walkthrough: Take the second, fourth, sixth and eighth letters.
explanation.definitionFit: To employ a tool or method is to put it into service, a plain synonym.

blocks.note: first meaning: a brad is a thin, small-headed tack used in woodwork
second meaning: to fasten or fix firmly

explanation.walkthrough: 'Brad' looks like a man's name; it is the carpenter's word for a slender tack.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is both a noun for a metal pin hammered into wood and a verb for fastening something in place.

clue.text: Sat about with our five pets

indicators.note: moved about means shifted around, so these letters are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A family sat around with its five animals.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pets' looks like animals in the scene, but it is the sense of favoured people, like the teacher's pet. 'Five' gives its letters, not V.
explanation.definitionFit: A teacher's pet is a favoured pupil, so pets in this sense are those given special preference.

indicators.note: an announcement is spoken out loud, so we want a word by its sound

blocks.note: a sub is a short-term advance of money

explanation.surface: A lone substitute is named for the team.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sub' looks like a substitute player, but in British usage a sub is a small advance or loan of cash.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words describe something that is solitary, on its own without others.

clue.text: A bit flighty, earsplitting, needing distance

indicators.note: a bit is a part of something, so the letters are a portion of the words that follow

blocks.note: the letters span the two words

explanation.surface: Someone a little giddy and very loud needs space from others.
explanation.walkthrough: The plural is fine as a distance: one is never enough between stars.
explanation.definitionFit: A light year is the distance light travels in a year, used for astronomical lengths.
